units.translation: where, since the scholiast has noted οὐ πτωχεύσεις [you will not be poor], Hermann wrote, with the words supplied by conjecture as the strophe shows they have fallen out, οὐ πενεῖ | καλλιπότμου τύχας · | ἱεροδόκα πέλει θεῶν λήματ᾽ ἀπ᾽ ἀνδρὸς ἁγνοῦ [he will not be poor in fortune of fair fate; she is the receiver of the gods' gifts from a pure man]. In which conjecture if there is any truth, πένει [he is poor] should be written, not πενεῖ [he will be poor], which is an unheard-of future form. But the present πένει [he is poor], since it could be used here for the future, could be interpreted by the scholiast as πτωχεύσεις [you will be poor], unless he wrote πτωχεύεις [you are poor]. Hermann correctly indicated the lacuna and restored λήματ᾽ [gifts], which had been changed by Turnebus and others to λήμματ᾽ [receipts], which I should not have retained under the entry λήμμα [receipt]. The scholiast noted: οἱ θεοὶ δέχονται τὰ ἀπὸ ἀνδρὸς ἁγνοῦ ἱερά [the gods receive the sacred offerings from a pure man].
The house does not know how to be poor.
For of the wise he is not poor.
revering the suppliant, where she is the receiver of the gods' gifts from a pure man.
he will not be poor in fortune of fair fate; she is the receiver of the gods' gifts from a pure man
the gods receive the sacred offerings from a pure man
commander of fifty ships five times
commander of fifty ships five times
mistress of the chorus of fifty Nereids
Thus Heath for πεντηκοστόπαις [having fifty children].
Thus from the apograph: πεντηκοντόπαις [having fifty children] M and Eustathius p. 37, 22.
He is a brother with fifty children.
It is properly of women, but by the tragedians it is not rarely assigned also to men.
where Heimsoeth rightly reads προστέρνων στολμῶν [of the garments before the breast], deleting the gloss πέπλων [of robes].
[πέπλοις μελαγχίμοις [with dark robes], which Eustathius p. 1254 cites from Aeschylus, no doubt refers to φάρεσιν μελαγχίμοις [with dark cloaks], which is read in Ch. 11.]
Of robes and garlands, if not now, when shall we have them for supplication?
And in linen robes a rent will fall.
taking him in robes with a dark-horned device she strikes
in woven robes of the Erinyes
You would call it a net and robes that entangle the feet.
And I alone was without a share of white-robed garments.
And in an endless robe she strikes, having bound the man with a cunning robe.
and the grips of my robes
I have cords and belts, fastenings of robes
he tears the robes around his body
and he was rending his folded robe
of the garments before the breast
λευκῶν ἐκ πεπλωμάτων ἰδεῖν [to see from white robes] Once in Sophocles Tr. 613. καινῷ πεπλώματι [with a new robe], and after these in Eustathius Opusc. p. 271, 88. 296, 26.
